facts.claim: In 2014, standing across from several hundred military special forces soldiers on a base in the Midwest, Brown defined vulnerability as the emotion we experience during uncertainty, risk and emotional exposure, and asked: 'Can you give me a single example of courage that you've witnessed in another soldier or experienced in your own life that did not require experiencing vulnerability?'
facts.source: AbeBooks book excerpt; groundedcuriosity review (p.23); giuseppemartinengo

facts.claim: The room fell completely silent ('Crickets'). A young soldier said: 'No, ma'am. Three tours. I can't think of a single act of courage that doesn't require managing massive vulnerability.'
Brown says she has since asked the question a couple of hundred times in meeting rooms around the world.

Brown contrasts armored leadership with daring leadership: armored leaders drive perfectionism and fear of failure, need to be the knower and be right, use power over people, and collect gold stars; daring leaders model healthy striving, aim to be learners and get it right, use power with people, and give gold stars.

Brown: 'When we get to the place that the armor is so thick that we no longer feel anything, we experience a real death.' And: 'Vulnerability is not winning or losing. It's having the courage to show up when you can't control the outcome.'

Brown's research for the book included interviews with 150 global C-level leaders, asked what (if anything) about the way people lead must change to succeed in a complex, fast-changing environment. The answer: 'We need braver leaders and more courageous cultures.'

Leaders named ten behaviors and cultural issues that get in the way of courage; the one ranked as the greatest concern was 'we avoid tough conversations, including giving honest, productive feedback.'
facts.source: Brown's own blog excerpt 'Clear is kind' (via search); Scribd preview listing it as item 01 (via search)

facts.claim: Some leaders attributed the avoidance to a lack of courage, others to a lack of skills, and more than half talked about a cultural norm of 'nice and polite' used as an excuse to avoid tough conversations.
facts.source: WebSearch summary of the book's research section

facts.claim: Brown's line: 'Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind.'

Living into values: Brown gives a list of more than 100 values and asks readers to narrow it to two core values ('if everything is a priority, nothing is'). Each value is then turned into three or four behaviors that support it and three or four slippery behaviors that move you out of it.
Brown's own two central values are faith and courage.
facts.source: Goodreads reader highlight of the book; Wharton interview with Adam Grant

facts.claim: Narrowing a long list to two is described as hard for almost everyone; most people identify with ten or twenty values.
Values must be translated into behaviors that can be 'taught, practiced, and evaluated'; Brown: living into our values means we do more than profess them, we practice them.

The book's subtitle is 'Brave Work. Tough Conversations. Whole Hearts.' The first skill set, 'rumbling with vulnerability', covers tough conversations in which we stay vulnerable, generous and curious.
Brown: 'Vulnerability is not winning or losing. It's having the courage to show up when you can't control the outcome.'

rejected.reason: The 150 leaders and the tough-conversations ranking are separate findings (f6, f7); 'seven years' is not verified for this study.
